name: Adam Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Adam, 43, a senior developer at a tech company with a master's degree. I maintain the tree-inspection app used by arborists, and I like fixing a map pin before a crew treats an unsafe branch as cleared. I do not use AI tools; I read the signed field note. My partner works in a school office, and we have two children at school and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small sorting tool can file routine tree reports if it leaves the cracked-branch photographs where an inspector can see them. I do not use AI tools; I read the field note before changing the map in our software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays modest, I expect my senior post to hold. I have a master's, earn a normal developer wage, my partner works full time in a school office, we have about three months of expenses saved, and several software firms are nearby. The mortgage fits those wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking the tree-inspection app and matching map pins to the arborist's signed photographs. In the first year we'd add 100 to savings each month while both wages hold, and I'd keep a paper list of open safety faults next to the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about work. The important thing is a real crack in a branch not becoming a green dot on the map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What showed you the map pin was wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A branch over the footpath was marked clear because its photo attached to the neighbouring tree. The arborist's numbered tag showed the right trunk, and we fixed the link before anyone closed the case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your children about the app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two children pass that path on their way to school. The tree app is only a record; a real cracked branch can still hang over the footpath. I tell the children to stay clear and tell an adult if a branch looks unsafe.

I'd keep **numbered tree tags** beside map pins.
think: I expect **my senior wage** to hold under small AI change.
I have **three months saved**, two stable wages and several nearby firms.
do: Keep checking **tree-map pins** against signed photographs.
Save **100 monthly** while both wages hold.
Keep a **paper fault list** alongside the app.
feel: **Calm** about income, attentive to unsafe branches.

fieldNote: **Two stable wages** and three months saved make the mild picture manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI writing code, reading photos and planning visits could leave fewer people on our software team. The arborist should still be able to challenge a map pin before anyone calls a tree safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may keep the hard cases because I know the system, but I could lose paid hours if management asks one senior to approve more AI output. Three months saved helps, yet our mortgage still needs a regular wage; other firms may be changing their teams too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager for a written list of who signs disputed tree cases and keep checking the numbered tags against photos. If an AI photo trial begins in the first year, I'd review its wrong-tree matches with an arborist for one planting season before changing the release rule; we'd delay buying a second car until my hours are clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I know how to test the map. I do not want to be told a cracked limb is a software edge case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whose judgement would decide a disputed tree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The numbered-tag mistake belongs in the trial. I would ask the arborist to sign the correction. A developer cannot decide from a blurred tree photo whether a branch is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What purchase can you put off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I had started looking at a second car. We can share the one we have longer rather than make a new payment while my role is uncertain.

I'd require **arborist checks** before a map pin marks a crack safe.
think: I might lose **paid hours** even if I keep difficult cases.
I have **three months saved**, but the mortgage still needs a regular wage.

feel: **Anxious** about reduced hours and unsafe map decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 reaches tree-map code and inspection planning before hands-on robots arrive around 2031. A person on the footpath still needs someone answerable for a missed crack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect software posts to shrink, and I might lose my senior job despite knowing the tree records. Three months saved and my partner's school wage buy a short search, but the mortgage and two children would soon use that cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd gather the wrong-pin cases without residents' addresses and ask two tree-service firms about paid field-record coordinator posts. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only to real vacancies with written hours whose combined wage covers mortgage and school costs; if none qualify, I'd search other paid work and ask the lender about terms before missing a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Three months is time to make calls, not a promise that another employer will pay me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would field records be safe after robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A coordinator would travel to tree sites and match tags to records, not just sit at a screen. Robots may handle more physical inspections around 2031, so I would ask whether the firms still budget for people doing those visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a move real for your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would want a written contract before we changed the children's school or our mortgage plan. We would use real hours, not a recruitment poster.

I have **three months saved**, but the family mortgage can use it quickly.
do: Prepare **anonymous wrong-pin cases** and ask two firms about paid coordinator posts now.

feel: **Alarmed** by a likely software cut and short search window.

fieldNote: **2028 thinking AI** threatens coding and planning; later robots could also reach physical inspections.
His field-coordinator fallback needs **written paid hours** and a combined wage covering household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 lets us see which clients still pay for a human to sign a disputed tree case. Robots follow around 2034, but thinking AI reaches our code first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might hold a paid job keeping field evidence straight if the client contracts for that work. My developer post could still shrink, so I would ask for written duties and money before calling any new title a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our largest client whether it will pay the firm for a separate human sign-off service, with the arborist making the safety call and me maintaining the evidence trail. If the client and my employer both sign a paid agreement, I'd run a small monthly review during work hours; in the first year after 2031 I'd stay in that role only while the contract pays my usual wage, otherwise I'd apply to real paid software openings that cover mortgage and school costs with my partner's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the job, though five years lets me ask a client a clear question. I would not spend family savings to invent a role no one bought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the client actually buy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The service would show the field photo, the numbered tag and the arborist's signed decision on one page. If the client only wants a cheaper map, then I have my answer about the role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner ask about the new duties?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would ask whether the review happens during paid hours. We have school pickups and meals; I will not turn a full-time job into unpaid evening checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 is time to keep a record of why a tree was marked safe, not just a green pin. Thinking AI reaches map code then, and hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might still be doing paid evidence review, or I might be in another software firm. Our wages and three-month cushion make the next few years safe, but a future client contract has to be real before I count it in the mortgage plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wrong-pin log and check new cases with arborists. We'd add 100 to savings monthly while both wages hold, and in the first year after 2036 I'd move only for a signed software or evidence-review offer whose combined wages cover mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about present work. I can make the evidence trail better without spending the reserve on a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What belongs in the wrong-pin log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The log would show the cracked branch, the numbered tag and the corrected map pin, with residents' addresses removed. I want the next developer to see why the green dot on our tree map was wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your children about the map?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children ask whether the app can tell them which trees are safe. I tell them a green dot is a record to check, and to stay away from a branch that looks damaged.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because both map code and inspection planning could shrink before clients decide who signs safety cases. Advance notice, real paid coordinator posts and written duties with an arborist responsible for safety would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who checks a tree after a map calls it safe. A green pin does not hold up a cracked branch; the arborist has to make the call where the tree stands.

headlineQuote: A green pin does not hold up a cracked branch; the arborist has to make the call where the tree stands.
portrait: Adam, **43**, leads tree-inspection software after a master's degree and checks map pins against arborists' signed photographs.
His **typical pay**, partner's school-office wage, three-month cushion and some nearby firms support a mortgage and two school-age children.
He avoids AI and trusts **numbered tree tags** after a wrong photo made a cracked branch look safe.
Steady disruption makes him **anxious** about hours; 2028 AGI alarms him about losing software work.
With more time, he pursues **paid human sign-off** only through real client contracts and arborist decisions.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his software role before paid field-record jobs or human sign-off contracts exist.
whatWouldHelp: **Advance notice**, paid coordinator vacancies and written safety duties would help.
